label: SCOTPOLY: systemic NSAID during acute dehydrating illness
title: Oral or rectal NSAID during acute dehydrating illness
statement: Step 5: Medication sick day guidance: advise to stop during dehydrating illness

plain_summary: A non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) taken by mouth or used as a suppository can increase the risk of acute kidney injury during a dehydrating illness. Check which pain medicines the person has actually taken, including occasional doses and products bought without a prescription. Review the sick-day plan and whether a temporary pause is appropriate. If a pause is agreed, review restarting once well and eating and drinking normally. Seek prompt medical review if symptoms persist or worsen or fluids cannot be kept down. NSAIDs can worsen heart failure. Decompensated heart failure needs urgent assessment, including review of NSAID use.

medicine_groups.name: Oral and rectal NSAIDs
medicine_groups.note: Count the listed NSAIDs taken by mouth, including combination tablets, or used as rectal suppositories. Examples include rectal diclofenac and indometacin. Check the form when a brand has more than one route, including Voltaren and Indocid. Indometacin may appear as indomethacin. Exclude low-dose aspirin, skin and eye preparations, injections and throat lozenges. Only oral Imflac tablets and Toradol 10 mg oral tablets count for those brands. Count supplies from the month of the newest dated record line and the two preceding calendar months, even if the directions say as directed or when needed. An unknown age does not prevent this check. An illness recorded only in a past episode leaves the current illness unknown. Check actual use at the counter.

needs_facts.meets: The patient currently has an acute dehydrating illness, such as repeated vomiting or diarrhoea, fever with sweats or shaking, or cannot keep fluids down.

options.words: Current dehydrating illness, such as repeated vomiting or diarrhoea, inability to keep fluids down, or other signs of dehydration
Fever with more than mild sweats or shaking
No current dehydrating illness, including recovery or mild illness with normal fluid intake

rule_for_models: At any age, look for a Group A NSAID supplied for oral or rectal use in the month of the newest record date or either of the two preceding months. With a qualifying supply, use the pharmacist's answer for this assessment, even if undated, or the latest relevant observation or condition that establishes current illness status. Confirm current dehydrating illness and cite the supply and illness lines. If status is missing, unknown or only describes a past episode, cite the supply and report a possible finding with Current dehydrating illness as the missing fact. Give no finding if there is no qualifying supply or the patient is well, has recovered or has only mild illness with normal fluid intake and no dehydration.
cannot_be_seen: A dispensing record may miss over-the-counter NSAIDs and supplies from other pharmacies. Check the route, recent use of as-needed pain relief, current symptoms and the sick-day plan with the patient.
ask_the_gp: Could you review the risk of acute kidney injury, whether the patient is still using the NSAID and whether a pause is appropriate and what pain relief is suitable during the illness? If the NSAID is still needed, when can the patient restart once well and eating and drinking normally? Could you advise on the sick-day plan and prompt review if symptoms persist or worsen? If heart failure is decompensated, could you arrange urgent assessment and review NSAID use?
